messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Tran was a widowed 75-year-old South Eastern Asian male who worked as a cybersecurity analyst. His life took a harrowing turn when his young child fell critically ill several years ago. The traumatic event of watching his child fight for their life in the hospital left an indelible mark on Mr. Tran’s psyche, and he now sought help to navigate through the distressing aftermath. The trauma was so vivid that even the slightest reminder could send him spiraling back into the depths of fear and horror. One day at work, while reading a report filled with clinical terms, he caught a whiff of antiseptic from a colleague who had recently been to the hospital. The smell instantly transported Mr. Tran back to the sterile environment where his child lay in critical condition. This olfactory trigger was potent because it was tied directly to the stark and terrifying moments he experienced there. Mr. Tran found that undergoing any medical examination or procedure could elicit a visceral reaction within him. Every time he had to visit a doctor, the fear of reliving those harrowing days would grip him tightly, making his heart race and his hands shake uncontrollably. The memory felt not just like a film but like something happening right now—his body reacting as if the stressful experience were actually unfolding again before his eyes. The recurrence of these triggers heightened Mr. Tran’s sense of threat. He was certain that any reminder of those days would unleash the same overwhelming negative emotions he had experienced during his child's illness. This fear made it difficult for him to seek medical care, even when necessary. For example, despite having chronic pain issues, he avoided going to doctors out of sheer dread. Mr. Tran’s memories were like a film that played over and over again in his mind. He would often find himself reliving the moments of panic and despair, unable to break free from the loop. These vivid recollections made it almost impossible for him to distinguish between past and present. When he tried to explain what had happened, he would get lost in the details, losing the thread of his narrative mid-sentence. The fear and physical reactivity associated with these triggers further reinforced his negative appraisals about the traumatic event itself. The memory of watching helplessly as his child battled for their life made every subsequent encounter with medical reminders a potent threat. This cycle tightened over time: each trigger reignited the memory, which in turn heightened his sense of threat and physical reactivity. One day, while at work, Mr. Tran received an email from a colleague about a new case involving hospital security breaches. The mention of hospitals and medical procedures immediately triggered a flashback, and he felt as if he were back in that sterile room with his child fighting for life. His hands trembled uncontrollably, and he could feel the panic rising within him. He realized then that these experiences were taking an immense toll on both his personal well-being and his professional capabilities. Mr. Tran had come to believe that avoiding any potential trigger was the only way to manage his distress, but this avoidance strategy had significant consequences. His work performance suffered as he found it increasingly difficult to focus amidst constant reminders of the hospital environment. He knew deep down that there must be a better way to cope with these memories and triggers. Ultimately, what finally brought Mr. Tran to seek help was a profound realization: he could no longer bear living in perpetual fear of reliving those harrowing days. His greatest hope was to regain control over his life and find ways to process the trauma without it dictating every aspect of his existence.
